# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 68 (Bu-Vb Pc68)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc68
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 68
**Title (English, from literature):** Not giving up a bad view
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 68, titled *Antarāyika*, regulates the formal correction of monastics who propagate pernicious doctrinal misconceptions [Hüsken 1997]. The rule stipulates that if a monk asserts that deeds declared by the Buddha to be obstructive (*antarāyikā dhammā*) are not actually obstructive, and persists in this wrong view after being formally admonished up to three times by the community, he incurs an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) [Wijayaratna 1990; Hüsken 1997]. In the Vinaya narrative framework (Vin IV 133–136), the rule originates from the conduct of the monk Ariṭṭha, who obstinately maintained that sensual pleasures do not constitute an obstacle, leading also to proceedings for his formal suspension (*ukkhepaniyakamma*) in the Khandhakas [Keown 1992; Dutt, Early Buddhist Monachism]. The disciplinary framework obliges monks to actively remonstrate with fellow monastics harboring erroneous opinions rather than leaving them unaddressed, and penalizes monks who associate with anyone suspended for refusing to relinquish such views [von Hinüber 1989; Wijayaratna 1990; Hüsken 1997]. An equivalent training rule exists for nuns as Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 146 [Wijayaratna 1990].

The account of Ariṭṭha's heresy constitutes one of the most prominent shared narratives in early Buddhist literature, corresponding closely to the *Alagaddūpama Sutta* (MN 22) and the *Kammakkhandhaka* (Cullavagga 11) [Keown 1992]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse between Bu-Vb Pc 68 and Kd 11 (sharing over 30,000 characters), MN 22 (nearly 28,000 characters), and related passages in MN 38 and Bu-Vb Pc 70 [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali tradition, this rule is universally represented across all surviving Vinaya traditions, with parallels preserved in Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, and Gāndhārī belonging to the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsaṅghika, and Kāśyapīya recensions. DharmaNexus also notes cross-language alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya commentaries, including the *Prātimokṣasūtraṭīkāvinayasamuccaya* and the *Prātimokṣasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. An English translation is available by Bhikkhu Brahmali.
